title: Functional Dependencies
relevance: SDE interviews and OAs use FDs to test whether you can reason about schema constraints, candidate keys, and dependency inference without memorizing normalization slogans.

phases.goal: Establish what an FD asserts, how trivial vs non-trivial FDs differ, and that validity is directional.

must_hit.point: X → Y means that if two tuples agree on X they must agree on Y; X is the determinant and Y the dependent.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the agreement condition on tuples and names determinant vs dependent.

must_hit.point: An FD is trivial when Y ⊆ X, and non-trivial when X ∩ Y = ∅.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives both subset and empty-intersection criteria correctly.

must_hit.point: In the Sid/Sname table, Sid → Sname is valid while Sname → Sid is invalid when the same name maps to different Sid values.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Uses the shared-name counterexample to show one direction holds and the reverse fails.

probes: What does X → Y mean for two rows of a relation, and when is that FD trivial?

hints.1: Think about what must be true whenever two tuples match on the left-hand attributes.
hints.2: Separate the formal agreement rule from the trivial/non-trivial classification rules.
hints.3: Say: same X implies same Y; trivial if Y ⊆ X; non-trivial if X ∩ Y is empty; Sid determines Sname but not vice versa when names collide.

phases.goal: Show how Armstrong's axioms, attribute closure, and candidate-key membership are used to infer and classify dependencies.

must_hit.point: Armstrong's primary axioms are reflexivity (Y ⊆ X ⇒ X → Y), augmentation (X → Y ⇒ XZ → YZ), and transitivity (X → Y and Y → Z ⇒ X → Z); they are sound and complete.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists the three primary rules and notes soundness plus completeness.

must_hit.point: Derived rules include union, decomposition, pseudo-transitivity, and composition; decomposition splits the RHS but the LHS of AB → C cannot be split into A → C or B → C.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names derived rules and explicitly refuses LHS decomposition.

must_hit.point: X⁺ is the set of all attributes functionally determined by X; a candidate key is a minimal attribute set whose closure is all attributes of R.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defines closure and minimality for candidate keys.

must_hit.point: A prime attribute belongs to some candidate key; a non-prime attribute belongs to none.

probes: Given a set of FDs, how do you compute an attribute closure and decide whether a set is a candidate key?

hints.1: Start from the attributes you already have and keep applying FDs whose left sides are covered.
hints.2: A set is a candidate key only if its closure is everything and no proper subset's closure is everything.
hints.3: Define X⁺, then check minimality; recall reflexivity, augmentation, and transitivity as the primary inference rules.

phases.goal: Apply closure and cover procedures to concrete FD sets: find keys, build a minimal cover, and test equivalence.

must_hit.point: For R(A,B,C,D) with {A → B, B → C, C → D}, only A⁺ is all attributes, so the candidate key is {A}; with the added D → A cycle, every singleton {A},{B},{C},{D} is a candidate key and all attributes are prime.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts the linear chain (key {A}) with the cycle (four singleton keys, empty non-prime set).

must_hit.point: For R(A,B,C,D,E) with {A → B, BC → D, E → C, D → A}, E never appears on any RHS so E is in every candidate key; the keys are {AE, BE, CE, DE}.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Uses the never-on-RHS heuristic for E and lists AE, BE, CE, DE.

must_hit.point: Minimal cover of {A → B, C → B, D → ABC, AC → D} is {A → B, C → B, D → A, D → C, AC → D} after splitting RHSs, keeping AC → D, and dropping redundant D → B.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Recalls single-attribute RHSs, no redundant LHS attributes, no redundant FDs, and the final set.

must_hit.point: FD sets X={AB → CD, B → C, C → D} and Y={AB → C, AB → D, C → D} are not equivalent because under Y, B⁺={B}, so Y does not derive B → C and does not cover X.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Checks mutual cover and fails Y covering X on B → C.

probes: Walk through finding all candidate keys for a relation, then either compute a minimal cover or decide whether two FD sets are equivalent.

hints.1: Look for attributes that never appear on a right-hand side—they must be in every key.
hints.2: For covers: split RHSs, test LHS attributes by closure without that FD, then drop FDs still implied by the rest.
hints.3: State the keys {AE,BE,CE,DE} or the minimal cover {A→B,C→B,D→A,D→C,AC→D}, and for equivalence show Y fails to derive B→C.

tradeoffs.topic: Decomposing the RHS vs decomposing the LHS
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Decomposition lets you split X → YZ into X → Y and X → Z, which is required for a minimal cover's single-attribute RHSs; you must not decompose the LHS—AB → C does not imply A → C or B → C.

tradeoffs.topic: Primary Armstrong axioms vs derived inference rules
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Reflexivity, augmentation, and transitivity are the sound and complete primary basis; union, decomposition, pseudo-transitivity, and composition are derived shortcuts that simplify computation without adding new inferential power.

gotchas.trap: Assuming that if X → Y holds then Y → X also holds.
gotchas.correction: FDs are directional; Sid → Sname can hold while Sname → Sid fails when one name maps to multiple Sid values.

gotchas.trap: Decomposing the left-hand side the same way as the right-hand side.
gotchas.correction: You may split the RHS of an FD into single attributes, but AB → C does not imply A → C or B → C.

gotchas.trap: Treating any determining set as a candidate key without checking minimality or full closure.
gotchas.correction: A candidate key must be minimal and its closure must contain every attribute of the relation; proper subsets must fail that test.

gotchas.trap: Declaring two FD sets equivalent after checking cover in only one direction.
gotchas.correction: X ≡ Y requires mutual cover: X covers Y and Y covers X; if B → C is in X but B⁺ under Y is only {B}, they are not equivalent.
